To greet people correctly depending on the time of day and the person.
To say where you’re from, your nationality and your job.
To use the verb ÊTRE (to be) with all persons.
To make negative sentences with ne… pas, and questions.
To know which letters are NOT pronounced at the end of words.
Ioana, an architect from Romania, is moving to Lyon for a new job. On the train she sits next to Julien.
Hello! Excuse me, is this seat free?
Thank you. My name is Julien. And you, what’s your name?
My name is Ioana. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you, Ioana. Where are you from?
I’m Romanian, I’m from Iași. And you?
Me, I’m French. I’m from Lyon. How are you?
No, I’m not a student. I’m an architect. And you?
Here’s Lyon! Goodbye, Ioana. Have a nice day!
Consonants at the end of a word are usually NOT pronounced: Paris = “Paree”, français = “frahn-SEH”, salut = “sah-LU”. A final “e” is silent too: architecte = “ar-shee-TEKT”.
The French U doesn’t exist in English. Say “ee” and, without moving your tongue, round your lips as for “oo”. You get a sound like the German “ü”.
OU is read like “oo” in “food”: oui = “wee”, bonjour = “bon-ZHOOR”, d’où = “doo”.
Nasal vowels: the air also comes out through the nose, and the “n” itself isn’t heard. Bonjour = “bõ-zhoor”, enchanté = “ã-shã-TAY”, bien = “byẽ”.
The French R is made in the throat, like gargling, not with the tip of the tongue. Try: merci, très, revoir.
É is a closed “e”, as in “day” (without the y). È and Ê are an open “e”, as in “bed”. French accent marks DON’T show the stressed syllable: the stress always falls on the last syllable.
1. How to greet: bonjour, bonsoir, salut
French has fewer greetings than English: “bonjour” covers both “good morning” and “good afternoon”.
with friends, any time (also when leaving)
In France it’s rude to walk into a shop or start a question without “bonjour”. The French say “Bonjour, madame” or “Bonjour, monsieur” even to the person at the bakery.
Have a nice day! (very common when parting)
2. Pronouns: je, tu, il, elle… and “vous”
As in English, French ALWAYS uses the pronoun. You can’t just say “suis Ioana”; you say “Je suis Ioana”. The French verb never stands alone.
becomes j’ before a vowel: j’aime
very common: on va = we’re going
several people OR one person, politely
ils is also used for a mixed group

“Moi” and “toi” are the stressed forms: “Moi, je suis français” = “ME, I’m French”. You use them on their own or for emphasis: “Et toi ?” = “And you?”. That’s exactly what Julien does in the dialogue.

“Tu” or “vous”? “Tu” is for friends, family, children and young colleagues. “Vous” is for strangers, at the bank, at the doctor’s, with your boss. Julien and Ioana are young, so they quickly switch to “tu”.
3. The verb ÊTRE = to be, step by step
ÊTRE means “to be”. As with “I am, you are, he is”, the form changes with the person. It’s the most important verb in French: learn it by heart.
“Es” and “est” sound the same: “eh”. Final letters are silent! Memory trick: SONT looks like “sound” without the d.
2) Where you’re from (city): I’m from Iași.
For “how are you?” French does NOT use ÊTRE but the set phrase “Ça va ? — Ça va bien, merci.” (word for word: “That goes? — It goes well”).
4. Job and nationality: no “a”, with masculine and feminine
Unlike English, after “être” jobs and nationalities have NO article: “Je suis architecte” (I’m an architect), not “Je suis une architecte”.
The feminine is usually made by adding -e. Sometimes the pronunciation changes, because the consonant before it is now heard:
Nationalities are written with a SMALL letter, unlike English: “je suis roumaine”. But the country has a capital: “la Roumanie”, “la France”.
5. Negation: NE … PAS, “not” in two pieces
In French, “not” has two parts that wrap around the verb: NE before, PAS after.
In fast speech the French often drop the “ne”: “Je suis pas étudiante”. You’ll hear it, but always write both parts.
The typical learner mistake: “Je ne suis étudiante” (without “pas”). Without “pas” the sentence is incomplete!

You politely ask an elderly lady: “Are you from Paris?”
